ui.qs: Tap the mic and say the word
ui.nm: No microphone here. Practice with pairs or dictation instead.

nasal.x: In “bon”, “blanc” and “vin” the n is not a consonant: it only sends the vowel through your nose. Do not touch the tongue to the roof of your mouth. Three sounds: on /ɔ̃/ with round lips (“bon”), an /ɑ̃/ with the mouth open (“blanc”), in /ɛ̃/ with spread lips (“vin”). “bon” and “banc” are two different words.

uou.x: French u /y/: say “ee” with the tongue forward, then round your lips as for “oo”: “tu”, “rue”. ou /u/ is a plain “oo”: “tout”, “roue”. One sound changes the word: “vu” (seen) and “vous” (you), “dessus” (above) and “dessous” (below).

r.x: The French r /ʁ/ is made at the back of the throat, like a soft, gentle gargle: the tip of the tongue rests behind the lower teeth and the back of the tongue rises. Try “rue”, “rouge” and “merci”. Do not roll it and do not curl the tongue. Compare “rue” and “lue”.

emuet.x: At the end of a word the letter e is silent: “porte”, “table”. In short words it is a quick, rounded /ə/: “je”, “demain”. Inside a word it often drops: “samedi” sounds like “samdi”. But a silent e still matters: it makes the last consonant heard, as in “petit” and “petite”, “grand” and “grande”.

eai.x: é /e/ is closed: lips spread, mouth almost shut, like a short “ay” with no glide: “été”, “café”. è, ê and ai /ɛ/ are more open, like the “e” in “bed”: “père”, “tête”, “lait”. The accent shows the sound. Dictation accepts missing accents (é è ê ç) but reminds you of them.

eu.x: eu has two sounds. At the end of a syllable it is closed /ø/: say “e” with your lips rounded as for “o”: “deux”, “peu”. Before a pronounced consonant, especially r, it is open /œ/: “heure”, “fleur”. Compare “peu” and “peur”, “jeu” and “jeune”.

liaison.x: French words flow together. A pronounced final consonant moves onto the next vowel (enchaînement). A silent final consonant is pronounced before a vowel (liaison): s and x become /z/, d becomes /t/. “les amis” sounds like /lezami/ and “vous avez” like /vuzave/. That is what separates “ils ont” from “ils sont”. No liaison before an aspirated h: “les héros”.

semi.x: Before a vowel, i, ou and u become quick glides inside one syllable. i is /j/ like the English “y”: “fille”. ou is /w/ like “w”: “oui”. u is /ɥ/, the lips of /y/ gliding: “huit”, “lui”, “nuit”. “huit” is one syllable, not “u-it”. Compare “loue” and “lui”, “fil” and “fille”.
